1345.title: Tears are mercy
1345.hook: the Prophet ﷺ wept at his son's death, and called tears a mercy (Bukhari)
1345.howItsDone: Muslims weep openly at deaths and funerals, citing the Prophet's tears at his son Ibrahim's death, while avoiding loud wailing, tearing clothes and words of protest against God's decree; his words about the eyes, the heart and the tongue are often recalled.

segments.voice: Yesterday, food for the bereaved: the dinner made for Ja'far's family, because grief keeps a household busy. Today, what to do when grief comes out as tears.

Even you, Messenger of Allah? The question comes from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf, one of the Prophet's companions, and Anas ibn Malik tells it in Sahih al-Bukhari. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, had a baby son named Ibrahim, nursed in the house of a blacksmith's family. Anas remembers the Prophet taking the boy, kissing him, holding him close. Some time later they went in again, and Ibrahim was dying. The Prophet's eyes filled, and the tears ran. His companion couldn't quite believe it. Even you?
screen: `EVEN YOU?` → `A BABY NAMED IBRAHIM.` → `THE PROPHET'S EYES FILLED.`

segments.voice: Some readers hear an old idea behind that question: the strong one doesn't cry, and whoever is closest to God should be calm, above all this. The Prophet's answer, in paraphrase, was simple: it is mercy. Then he wept more, and said, again in paraphrase: the eyes shed tears and the heart grieves, but we say only what pleases our Lord, and we are saddened by your parting, Ibrahim. Three parts. The eyes are allowed to cry. The heart is allowed to grieve. And the tongue is held: it says only what pleases God. The line isn't between crying and not crying. It's between grief and protest. In another hadith in al-Bukhari, the Prophet's young grandchild is dying, and again his eyes overflow. Sa'd ibn 'Ubadah asks what this is. The answer, paraphrased: this is mercy that Allah has put in the hearts of His servants, and Allah is merciful to those of His servants who are merciful. So tears aren't a weakness to be forgiven. They're the mercy itself, showing. The same collection has the Prophet disowning, in paraphrase, those who slap their cheeks, tear their clothes and cry out with the wailing of the old days. Weeping, yes. Wailing that rages against what God has decreed, no. A heart that breaks, and a tongue that stays kind.
screen: `EVEN YOU?` · `IT IS MERCY.` · `EYES WEEP, HEART GRIEVES, TONGUE IS KIND.` · `WEEPING, YES. WAILING, NO.`

segments.voice: Is there a loss you've been holding tight, keeping composed about: a person, a place, a time of life? Let it come up gently; if tears come, they come, and if they don't, that's fine too, just don't push it back down. If you pray, you can hold the Prophet's words: the eyes weep, the heart grieves, and the tongue says only what pleases the Lord. If grief ever brings thoughts of harming yourself, please call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency number.
Tears are mercy. The Prophet's answer when asked why he wept at his son's death: the tears are a mercy God places in the heart. Today's word.
Your line: tears are mercy. Even the Prophet's eyes filled for his son. Until tomorrow.

1346.title: Visiting graves
1346.hook: visit graves, for they remind of the hereafter (Muslim)
1346.howItsDone: Muslims visit the graves of family and of the community, citing the hadith in Sahih Muslim where the Prophet lifted an earlier ban and said graves remind of death; visitors greet the dead, remember them and pray for them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, tears are mercy: the Prophet's tears for his son Ibrahim, and a tongue that stays kind. Today, the place people go back to, long after the funeral.

For a while, it was forbidden. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, had at first told his followers not to visit graves. Then, in a hadith in Sahih Muslim, he reverses it, in Buraydah's report, in paraphrase: I had forbidden you to visit graves; now visit them. A rule given, then lifted out loud, with the change left on the record for everyone to see. Why visiting the dead was opened up again, and what a graveyard is for.
screen: `AT FIRST, FORBIDDEN.` → `I HAD FORBIDDEN YOU.` → `NOW VISIT THEM.`

segments.voice: The texts don't spell out why the first rule was given. Some readers suggest the early community was close to old customs of loud lament and worship at tombs, and needed distance from them first. That's an explanation people offer, not something the hadith says. What the hadith does give is the reason for the opening. In another report in Sahih Muslim, from Abu Hurayrah, the Prophet visited the grave of his own mother. He wept there, and the people around him wept. And he said, in paraphrase: visit graves, for they remind you of death. Some other collections carry the wording: they remind you of the hereafter. Either way, notice who the visit is for. Not mainly the dead. The visitor. Each stone is a person who once had plans for next week. A name. Flowers someone left. A path worn by other visitors. And there's love in it too: a son, grown and leading a community, crying at his mother's grave. He didn't treat the grave as a place to avoid. He went, he wept, and then he opened the door for everyone else to go. So a cemetery isn't only a place for the dead. It's a classroom for the living, with very quiet teachers.
screen: `WHY FORBIDDEN? THE TEXT IS QUIET.` · `HIS MOTHER'S GRAVE.` · `THEY REMIND YOU.` · `A CLASSROOM FOR THE LIVING.`

segments.voice: Think of a grave you know, a grandparent's, a friend's, a stranger's stone you once noticed on a walk, and stand there in your mind for a few breaths. Ask what it reminds you of, and what you'd want to say. If you pray, you can remember the person who lies there.
Visiting graves. Once forbidden, then opened by the Prophet himself: go, because the graves remind you. Today's word.
Your line: they remind. Quiet teachers, every one of them. Go gently.

1347.title: The greeting to the dead
1347.hook: peace upon you, people of these dwellings (Muslim)
1347.carry: peace upon you, people of the graves
1347.howItsDone: When Muslims enter a graveyard, they greet the dead with the words the Prophet taught, beginning "as-salamu 'alaykum, ahl ad-diyar", and ask God's well-being and mercy for those buried there and for themselves.

segments.voice: Yesterday, visiting graves: once forbidden, then opened, because they remind. Today, what you say when you get there.

It's night in Madinah, and 'A'ishah is awake when her husband gets up. In a long hadith in Sahih Muslim, she tells how the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, slipped out quietly, and she followed him through the dark to al-Baqi', the graveyard. He stood there a long time, raised his hands three times, and turned back. She hurried home ahead of him, out of breath, and he asked what was wrong. It all came out. Then she asked the question underneath it: what should I say to them, when I go there?
screen: `NIGHT IN MADINAH.` → `HE GOES TO AL-BAQI'.` → `WHAT SHOULD I SAY TO THEM?`

segments.voice: He told her. And in another report in Sahih Muslim, from Buraydah, he taught the same words to his companions when they went out to the graves. They begin: as-salamu 'alaykum, ahl ad-diyar. Peace be upon you, people of these dwellings. Then, in paraphrase: you who are believers and Muslims, and we, if God wills, will be joining you. And it asks God for well-being, for us and for you. As-salamu 'alaykum is the greeting Muslims give the living: at the door, in the street, at the close of the prayer. Here it's said to the dead, in the same words, the way you'd greet a neighbor. And the graves are called dwellings. Homes. The people buried there are residents, and you're a visitor in their neighborhood. Then the honest middle line: we will be joining you. Nobody pretends otherwise. The visitor and the visited are on the same road, at different points along it. The last line asks well-being for both at once. The living don't stand above the dead, praying down at them; they stand beside them and ask together. In 'A'ishah's version the Prophet also asks mercy for those who have gone ahead and those who come later. One greeting, and the whole line of people, before and after, is inside it.
screen: `AS-SALAMU 'ALAYKUM, AHL AD-DIYAR.` · `THE SAME GREETING AS THE LIVING.` · `WE WILL BE JOINING YOU.` · `FOR US, AND FOR YOU.`

segments.voice: Say the opening quietly a few times, until it sits easily: as-salamu 'alaykum, ahl ad-diyar, peace be upon you, people of these dwellings. Then think of a graveyard you know and the people resting there, named or unnamed. If you pray, you can offer them the greeting as it was taught; if not, simply hold them in mind as neighbors on the same road.
The greeting to the dead. Peace be upon you, people of these dwellings: the Prophet's words for greeting those in their graves. Today's word.

1348.title: What continues
1348.hook: three things continue: ongoing charity, useful knowledge, a righteous child's prayer (Muslim)
1348.howItsDone: Muslims fund wells, mosques, schools, trees and copies of the Qur'an as sadaqah jariyah, ongoing charity, sometimes in a dead relative's name, citing the hadith in Sahih Muslim on the three things that continue after death.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the greeting to the dead: peace upon you, people of these dwellings, and we will be joining you. Today, what still moves after a life stops.
screen: `PEACE UPON YOU, PEOPLE OF THE GRAVES.`

segments.voice: Three people, all of them gone. One dug a well; nobody drawing water from it now remembers her name, but the water still comes up every morning. One explained something hard to a student, who explained it to another, until it reached someone who never met him. One raised a child, who now says a parent's name in prayer, alone at night. Each has died, and the thing they started hasn't stopped. In Islam, a hadith names three things like these.
screen: `A WELL STILL GIVING WATER.` → `AN EXPLANATION STILL PASSED ON.` → `A CHILD STILL PRAYING.`

segments.voice: Abu Hurayrah reports it, in Sahih Muslim. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, said, in paraphrase: when a person dies, their deeds come to an end, except for three. Ongoing charity. Knowledge that people benefit from. And a righteous child who prays for them. The first sentence is stark. Deeds end. Whatever a person meant to do tomorrow stays undone. Then the word except, and three doors left open. Ongoing charity is sadaqah jariyah in Arabic, charity that flows, like running water: not the coin given once, but the thing that keeps giving after the giver is gone, a well, a tree whose fruit people eat, a school, a copy of the Qur'an someone reads from. The second is knowledge that benefits: not knowledge you merely had, but knowledge passed on and still useful, a recipe, a skill, a way of being kind a student learned by watching you. The third, a righteous child who prays for you, turns the arrow around. The parent can't do anything more. The child keeps praying, and in the hadith, that still counts for the one who raised them. What do the three share? Each lives inside other people: the water in someone else's cup, the understanding in someone else's head, the prayer in someone else's mouth. Some readers put it this way: what continues, in this hadith, is what was passed on to someone else.
screen: `WHEN A PERSON DIES, DEEDS END.` · `EXCEPT FOR THREE.` · `CHARITY, KNOWLEDGE, A CHILD'S PRAYER.` · `WHAT CONTINUES IS WHAT YOU GAVE.`

segments.voice: Let the three come by, one at a time: something that could keep giving after you, something you know that could help someone if you taught it, and the people who might one day remember you in prayer. Pick just one, and think of the first small step.

1349.title: Praying for the dead
1349.hook: the living pray for the dead, and the Qur'an is recited for them in many communities
1349.howItsDone: Muslims make du'a for their dead, using words like those in Qur'an 14:41 and 59:10, and give charity in their names; in some communities people also gather to recite the Qur'an, sometimes surah Ya Sin, though scholars differ on whether the reward of recitation reaches the dead.

segments.voice: Yesterday, what continues: ongoing charity, knowledge that benefits, and a child who prays. Today, that third door, opened wide.

A man came to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, worried about his mother. She had died suddenly, he said, and he thought that if she'd had the chance to speak, she would have given something in charity. So: if I give charity for her now, will it reach her? The Prophet said yes. 'A'ishah tells it, in Sahih al-Bukhari. A son, too late for one last conversation, asking if there's still a way to do something for her. And being told there is.
screen: `HIS MOTHER DIED SUDDENLY.` → `WILL IT REACH HER?` → `YES.`

segments.voice: That yes is the floor this day stands on: in Islam, the living can still do something for the dead. The first thing, the one anyone can do, is du'a, a personal prayer asking God for them. The Qur'an gives words for it. In surah Ibrahim, the prophet Abraham prays, in Pickthall's translation: "Our Lord! Forgive me and my parents and believers on the day when the account is cast." And in surah al-Hashr, those who came later in the faith say: "Our Lord! Forgive us and our brethren who were before us in the faith." Me, my parents, the believers, the ones who went before. The prayer holds the whole line at once. The funeral prayer is itself a du'a for the one who died. The greeting at the graves asks well-being for the dead. And yesterday's hadith counts a child's prayer among the things that keep reaching a person. Then there's the Qur'an recited for the dead. In some communities, people gather after a death to recite, and some read surah Ya Sin. Here the scholars have differed. Some hold that the reward of recitation can be given to the dead and reaches them. Others hold to what the hadith name directly, such as du'a and charity, and are cautious about more. Both views draw on the texts, and on love for the dead. The plainest part is shared by both: remember them, and ask God for them.
screen: `WILL IT REACH HER? YES.` · `DU'A: ASKING GOD FOR THEM.` · `ME, MY PARENTS, THE BELIEVERS.` · `RECITATION: THE SCHOLARS DIFFER.`

segments.voice: Let one person who has died come to mind, say their name quietly, and remember one specific thing about them: a laugh, a phrase, a meal. If you pray, you can use Abraham's words from surah Ibrahim, Our Lord, forgive me and my parents and the believers, or the words from al-Hashr for those who were before us. If you don't pray, simply remember them with care.
Praying for the dead. Du'a and charity offered for those who have died, which the hadith says can still reach them. Today's word.

1350.title: Writing a will
1350.hook: a Muslim shouldn't spend two nights without a written will (Bukhari)
1350.howItsDone: Muslims are encouraged to keep a written will, a wasiyyah, citing the hadith of Ibn 'Umar in al-Bukhari; bequests outside the fixed shares of inheritance are limited to a third of the estate, following the hadith of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas.

segments.voice: Yesterday, praying for the dead: du'a and charity that can still reach them. Today, something the living can do for the ones they'll leave behind.

Two nights. That's the window in this hadith, and it's short on purpose. 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar reports it, in Sahih al-Bukhari: the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, said, in paraphrase, that it isn't right for a Muslim who has something to leave in a will to spend two nights without that will written down and kept with them. Not someday, once things settle down. Two nights. And in Sahih Muslim, Ibn 'Umar adds what he did about it: from the time he heard those words, not a single night passed without his will beside him.
screen: `TWO NIGHTS.` → `WRITTEN, AND KEPT WITH YOU.` → `NOT A NIGHT WITHOUT IT.`

segments.voice: The word is wasiyyah: a will, a bequest, and also a charge, the last instructions you leave in someone's care. In surah al-Baqarah, those near death who leave wealth are told to make a bequest for parents and near relatives, fairly, as a duty on those who are mindful of God. The Qur'an also names fixed shares for heirs, in surah al-Nisa, which is tomorrow's story. The wasiyyah is the part a person shapes for themselves, and a hadith puts a limit on it. Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas tells it, also in al-Bukhari. He was ill, and the Prophet came to visit. Sa'd said he had wealth, and only a daughter to inherit, and asked: may I give away all of it in my will? No. Half? No. A third? And the Prophet said, in paraphrase: a third, and a third is a lot. It's better to leave your heirs well off than to leave them poor, holding out their hands to people. So a will carries two loves at once: for the causes and people outside the family, and for the family, who shouldn't be left in need. Why the hurry? The hadith doesn't say. One way to hear it: nobody knows which night is the last. A will written today isn't gloomy. It's kind. The people you love won't spend their grief guessing, or arguing, about what you wanted.
screen: `WASIYYAH: A WILL, A CHARGE.` · `SA'D ASKS: ALL OF IT?` · `A THIRD, AND A THIRD IS A LOT.` · `NOBODY KNOWS WHICH NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Ask yourself: if this were my last night, what would the people I love need to know? Where things are kept, who should be looked after, any debt to repay or promise to keep, any cause you'd want to share in what you leave. Where you live, the law may have its own requirements, so this is only the first page of a will, in your head.

1351.title: Inheritance, lived
1351.hook: dividing an estate by the shares, with fairness and peace
1351.howItsDone: Muslims divide an estate according to the shares set out in surah al-Nisa, after debts and any bequest are settled, and Qur'an 4:8 asks that relatives without a share, orphans and the needy who are present be given something and spoken to kindly.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the wasiyyah: a will kept close, and Sa'd's third, because a third is a lot. Today the week closes at a family table, where what's left gets divided.

Who gets what? After a funeral, that question can arrive at the kitchen table along with a folder of papers, a cousin who flew in, and tea nobody drinks. Old hurts can come up with it. Who did more. Who was favored. And sometimes the person who used to settle things is the one who is gone. The Qur'an walks straight into that room. It doesn't leave the dividing to whoever argues hardest. It names the shares itself.
screen: `A TABLE, A FOLDER, A FAMILY.` → `WHO DESERVES WHAT?` → `THE QUR'AN NAMES THE SHARES.`

segments.voice: Surah al-Nisa opens the subject with a principle, in paraphrase: men have a share of what parents and near relatives leave, and women have a share of what parents and near relatives leave, whether it's little or much, a share that's fixed. Women named in the same sentence as men. The verses that follow set out the shares in detail: children, parents, spouses, brothers and sisters, each with a portion. And they end by calling these the limits set by God. So the hardest question at that table is already answered. Nobody has to win the argument. But a verse just before the detailed shares makes this lived, not just calculated. In Pickthall's translation: "And when kinsfolk and orphans and the needy are present at the division (of the heritage), bestow on them therefrom and speak kindly unto them." Look who's in the room: relatives with no fixed share, an orphan, someone poor standing at the edge. Give them something, and speak kindly. The math is exact. The manners around it are generous. Now the week: tears the Prophet called mercy, graves that remind, a greeting that calls them dwellings, three things that continue, charity that still reaches, a will written before the second night, and now the shares, divided with fairness and kind words. Each is a way the living keep faith with the dead, and with each other, after the funeral is over.
screen: `A SHARE FOR MEN, A SHARE FOR WOMEN.` · `THE LIMITS SET BY GOD.` · `GIVE TO THOSE PRESENT, AND SPEAK KINDLY.` · `KEEPING FAITH AFTER THE FUNERAL.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind your own family, or one you know well, and notice any old question of who got what, or who was favored, that still sits between people; you don't have to solve it. Then think of the verse's two parts, the share that's due and the kind word, and ask where a kind word could go, even if nothing else changes. If you pray, you can remember that family with care.
Inheritance. The shares the Qur'an sets for heirs in surah al-Nisa, divided with fairness, with something for those present, and with kind words. Today's word.
Your line: shares with peace. A share that's due, and a kind word with it. That's the week.
